title: Whose Circle Was It Anyway
standfirst: Fernand Léger painted his disc pictures in the year after a mustard-gas attack nearly killed him at Verdun. The shape itself, though, he almost certainly took from somewhere — or someone — else, and the record never quite settles the question of how much he owed and to whom.

sections.heading: Two Painters, One Shape, No Settled Answer
sections.body:
Robert and Sonia Delaunay had been painting pure circular abstractions — the Disques, the Formes circulaires cosmiques — since 1912 and 1913, chasing rhythm and depth through overlapping arcs of colour with almost mystical intent behind them. Léger had known that language before the war; the museum that now holds the closest sibling to this picture says so plainly. When he returned to painting discs himself in 1918, the resemblance was not incidental, and one likely conduit was a book: Blaise Cendrars' war narrative J'ai Tué, published in November 1918 with illustrations by Léger, put him back in the Delaunays' orbit at almost exactly the moment the disc reappeared in his own work.

What the record does not do is call this a theft, a feud, or even, really, a rivalry. Léger's discs read differently from the Delaunays' — his curators describe them as bare 'pictorial motif of colours and planar forms,' stripped of the cosmic ambition Robert Delaunay claimed for the same shape. Whether that difference amounts to a real departure or a polite distance from a debt he'd rather not spell out is a question nobody involved settled on paper, and it's worth resisting the urge to settle it here either.

sections.heading: What Three Years in the Argonne Actually Did to Him
sections.body:
Léger was mobilised in August 1914 and spent close to three years at the front, first as a sapper in the Argonne, then as a stretcher-bearer. He had almost no time to paint, so he drew instead, on whatever was at hand — military maps, ammunition boxes — sending sketches of bombed ground and mutilated bodies home to his wife. In September 1916 a German mustard-gas attack at Verdun nearly killed him and put him in hospital.

What he took from the experience was not despair so much as a recalibration of what fear even was. He later said the war had shifted fear from something visual, provoked by an enemy's face, to something purely acoustic — the sound of the guns doing the work dread used to need a sight of the enemy to do. He went further: the war's method struck him as unimaginative and linear as a geometry problem, purer as abstraction, he said, than Cubism itself. A working Cubist had just watched an artillery barrage out-abstract him.

sections.heading: The Breech of a 75-Millimetre Gun
sections.body:
Léger dated his own turn to a specific, almost absurdly small observation: the sight of the breech of a 75-millimetre gun, open in the sunlight, next to the men working it. He described what followed as trading abstraction for 'painting in slang' — plain, mechanical, object-based. Convalescing after the gas attack, he painted The Card Players in 1917, its figures reduced to jointed, tubular near-robots, still visibly working through what the front had done to how he saw bodies.

The disc pictures that followed in 1918 and 1919, this one among them, read as the same instinct turned toward order rather than damage. One closely related canvas, dated October 1918 and shown that February at Léonce Rosenberg's Galerie l'Effort Moderne, carries what its curators call oblique references to movement and to the colours of flags — an Armistice picture, more or less, in the same bright, machined vocabulary he'd been developing since the breech of that gun caught his eye.

sections.heading: From the Trenches to Le Corbusier's Drawing Board
sections.body:
Léger married Jeanne-Augustine Lohy in December 1919 and, the following year, struck up a friendship with Le Corbusier that pulled his machine-age painting toward Purism — Le Corbusier and Amédée Ozenfant's cooler, more mathematical answer to Cubism's improvisation. Through the 1920s his 'mechanical' figures softened into the calmer, more populated paysages animés, and by 1924 he had all but set painting aside for film, co-directing the experimental Ballet Mécanique with George Antheil, Man Ray and Dudley Murphy — close-ups of ordinary objects cut to a rhythm borrowed straight from the machine imagery of his paintings. From 1924 he taught at the Académie Moderne, which he had co-founded with Ozenfant.

The disc, as a motif, largely stayed behind in 1919. What he kept from it was the underlying premise: that an object — a gun breech, a circle of paint, a piston — could carry a painting's whole meaning without a human figure to explain it.

sections.heading: An American Decade, a Party Card, and a Mural at the UN
sections.body:
Léger spent the Second World War in the United States, teaching at Yale and then Mills College, and found new material in the country's cast-off machinery: rusting engines with flowers growing up through them, birds perched on abandoned metal, a contrast he made central to paintings like The Tree in the Ladder. He credited Broadway's neon signs with changing how he handled colour — a figure would 'turn blue,' he said, then the light would fade and another sign would 'turn him red or yellow,' colour arriving from outside the object rather than belonging to it.

He returned to France in 1945 and joined the Communist Party, and his late work turned toward monumental scenes of ordinary labour and leisure — builders, acrobats, divers, a country outing — work one historian has called the product of a 'passionate humanist' rather than a doctrinaire one. In 1952 his murals went up in the UN General Assembly Hall. He died suddenly at his home in Gif-sur-Yvette on 17 August 1955, three years before the house itself, willed to the Communist Party, hosted the negotiations that ended the Paris Peace Accords.
